A major challenge for achieving reliable data transmission in this system is the distortion caused by chromatic dispersion, resulting in four spectral nulls in the signal. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer is employed, but its effectiveness is limited due to the propagation of burst errors. A weighted DFE can mitigate this issue, but its performance is further enhanced when combined with maximum likelihood sequence estimation. Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.

massive arc-like structure on the sky at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 gigaparsec in size, this structure, known as the Giant Arc, appears almost symmetrical on the sky and was discovered through the presence of magnesium II absorbers in the spectra of background quasars. Utilizing magnesium II absorbers offers a novel approach to investigating large-scale structures at redshifts between 0.45 and 2.25. We present the observational characteristics of the Giant Arc and evaluate its statistical significance using three distinct methods: hierarchical clustering, the Cuzick-Edwards test, and power spectrum analysis. Each of these approaches has unique attributes and provides compelling evidence when considered collectively. To address potential biases in our analysis, we employed strategies to mitigate post-discovery significance assessments. Our findings indicate that the Giant Arc exhibits an overdensity of approximately 1.3, with a margin of error of 0.3. This structure is part of a growing collection of massive large-scale structures that may challenge the cosmological principle, which underlies the standard model of cosmology. The Giant Arc could be a precursor to a structure like the Sloan Great Wall, but on a much larger scale, observed when the universe was half its current age.

using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention. Two primary approaches, direct methods and two-stage pipelines, can be distinguished based on whether intermediate cues are employed. In the latter category, CNNs first regress intermediate cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points in the initial stage. These intermediate cues then facilitate the computation of object pose through constructed correspondence constraints. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by integrating two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. We begin by utilizing a local patch-based method to generate projection heatmaps, representing the confidence distribution of projected 3D bounding box corners. A projection grouping module is then introduced to eliminate redundant local maxima from heatmaps. In contrast to directly applying the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Ultimately, the proposed framework selects correspondences with higher confidence to determine object pose, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments on three public datasets.

This library builds upon the Graphical Lasso method, initially introduced in (Friedman 2007), which estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the name Covariance Selection, the framework has been expanded to include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012) and more recently to jointly estimate multiple inverse covariance matrices, as seen in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package supports the solution of a general formulation, encompassing significant special cases, including the single Graphical Lasso with latent variables, the Group, and the Fused Graphical Lasso.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, the authors' previous work on sampling accuracy has been expanded upon, allowing for the identification of stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, certain schemes yield exact configurational averaging results, potentially leading to improved performance in biomolecular modeling, where bond stretches play a significant role. In general systems, an optimal method can be identified that exhibits very low bias in comparison to other alternatives. The results of simulations on the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) show that higher accuracy is achieved without compromising computational efficiency, allowing for large timesteps and maintaining the conformational exploration rate. The optimal scheme proves to be a superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering efficiency improvements of 25% or more in practical timestep sizes in vacuum and reductions in configurational average errors by a factor of ten or more in solvated simulations at large timesteps.

Through the examination of extensive categories of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify the potential generalized global symmetries present and investigate the mechanisms that circumvent them. Key components of such effective field theories include generalized $\theta$-terms, which introduce non-linear interactions between axion fields and topological terms that are quadratic in gauge field strengths and lead to the breaking of numerous global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can lead to the breaking of residual global symmetries. However, our findings reveal that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms results in a generalized Witten effect, implying that the spectrum of charged states is composed of an infinitely populated grid. We demonstrate that this grid is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation, which characterizes the boundary of the moduli space near which the effective theory is defined.

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds.

Our adversary model assumes a sophisticated opponent who can manipulate the reward and transition at any step within an episode, but only up to a certain percentage of episodes. Our model is more aggressive than previous approaches. We initially demonstrated that no algorithm can find a significantly better policy than one that is slightly suboptimal, given our attack model. multi-phonon physics, is being explored for its potential applications in metrology and on-chip communication, among other areas. Quantum acoustic resonators, or cavities, are being utilized to investigate multi-phonon phenomena both theoretically and experimentally. We investigate a system consisting of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity. This system has exhibited intriguing multi-phonon effects, but previous descriptions have been limited to a two-level quantum dot model. This limitation restricts the complexity of a true semiconductor quantum dot. In this study, we propose a model that accounts for both bright and dark excitons in the quantum dot, with dark excitons being particularly useful due to their low decoherence rates. By fine-tuning the laser frequency, we demonstrate the ability to achieve giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles. Notably, we can create dark states in the quantum dot without an external magnetic field and, in a dissipative scenario, the system can function as a phonon gun emitting N-phonon bundles.

lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse or move within the first Brillouin zone along high-symmetry paths. Additionally, applying a dimerization of the hopping terms also moves the Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along high-symmetry paths. This research could provide insights into recent observations of Dirac cones in hBN-MDC core shells and be generalized to describe quasiparticles in doped hBN. Furthermore, we propose a potential implementation using CO coupled hBN by exploiting the charge-3 nature of CO and suitable tuning of the two-dimensional lattice's symmetry-breaking parameters.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. This occurs when a coherent state and a single-photon state are input into a beam splitter or parametric amplifier, and a single photon is detected in one of the output channels. The probabilities of successful detection differ depending on whether a beam splitter or parametric amplifier is used. We have also demonstrated that the SPCCSs generated by these two methods are identical, based on an analysis of their photon number distributions. Furthermore, we have thoroughly investigated the quantum properties of SPCCSs, including their non-Poissonian distribution, anti-bunching effect, quadrature squeezing effect, and the negativity of their Wigner function. These findings confirm that SPCCSs are non-Gaussian states that exhibit an abundance of non-classical behavior, and as such, they possess quantum advantages that can be leveraged for various technological applications.

However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilators being shared between multiple patients by modeling the ventilator as a source term in the lung's flow dynamics. We also examined different ventilator configurations, including single and dual-ventilator setups with varying patient masses, ventilator flow rates, lung compliance, and resistance. Our results showed that our approach can accurately predict pressures and flow rates in the lungs using very few data points, and ventilator sharing does not significantly affect patient breathing rates.

CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To overcome this, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. This study investigates whether it's possible to automate the process of segmenting esophageal tumors from CT scans alone. To achieve this, we developed a fully automatic method based on convolutional neural networks, called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), which focuses on the most relevant features and regions. We tested this method on a large dataset of 792 scans from 288 patients with varying anatomies and conditions, and the results showed a high degree of accuracy with a simplified clinical workflow. Our code is available for public use.

and often hydrocarbons are found in intricate reservoir formations. To optimize production from these complex reservoirs and minimize costs, accurate real-time well placement (geosteering) is essential. Geosteering typically relies on up-to-date formation evaluations while drilling, obtained through the interpretation of well logs in real-time. For this application, a reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to analyze well logs and capture geological uncertainties in real-time is necessary. An integrated iterative ensemble-based method, specifically the approximate Levenberg Marquardt form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML), is employed in this study to build an ensemble of geological models, representing possible formation configurations around the well path. The ensemble is created by minimizing a data misfit function and a regularization term using a limited memory Broyden formulation. The main challenge in this study lies in handling multiple formations along the well path. A common approach involves stacking the well logs from different formations, assuming they cross-interact, which can lead to an ill-conditioned Hessian matrix and slow convergence. To overcome this, a more realistic approach is proposed here by treating the formations separately and combining the results in a physical sense, inspired by the multiple pointing version of the Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo sampler. The proposed method is computationally efficient and robust, as demonstrated in a synthetic case with three formations, where the time taken to generate the ensemble was approximately 2 hours on 64 CPUs. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling.

problems in arithmetic geometry, specifically to counting curves and their intersections in certain types of fields. We test our methods using a particular problem related to a type of curve called a plane quartic, and we look at how the geometry of this curve changes when we view it in different ways. We express the reasons why certain curves and their intersections may not behave well in terms of how their shapes change when viewed in different ways. We also show how to calculate the importance of certain curves and their intersections in terms of their shapes and the way they are defined. This allows us to confirm a prediction made by other mathematicians about the importance of certain types of curves and their intersections in certain types of fields. Our results rely on a theorem that helps us understand how the geometry of fields changes when we view them in different ways.

Microwave Background (CMB) could serve as evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) model, which proposes the universe undergoes cycles of expansion and contraction. These patterns include low-variance circles resulting from black hole mergers and Hawking points resulting from black hole evaporation. A recent study used machine learning software called HawkingNet to search for Hawking points in the CMB, but found no statistically significant evidence. Similarly, a high-resolution search for low-variance circles in the Planck and WMAP CMB data revealed no significant results after removing anomalies. However, the absence of distinct features in the CMB does not necessarily disprove CCC, as a large density of such patterns could produce a non-Gaussian fluctuation in the CMB. Interestingly, the real CMB sky exhibits significant local deviations from Gaussian noise on a local scale, according to the best-fit Lambda-CDM and COM PowerSpect CBM TT-full power spectra.

However, these conic formulations frequently come encoded with unnecessary variables and constraints, resulting from an often-used method of applying dualization techniques to derive their development. This paper introduces a decoding process that can efficiently strip away excess elements from a conic formulation, thereby making it more efficient for use with solvers like Gurobi or MOSEK. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that its proposed decoding process meets specific optimality criteria, specifically for certain restricted cases of its application.

Object detectors that use deep learning process context differently in scene recognition. 
In this study, we classify object detectors into three types based on context usage: 
those that don't use context by isolating the input (RCNN), those that use partial context by isolating the feature map (two-stage methods), and those that use full context without any isolation (single-stage methods). 
We examine how context affects each deep detector category systematically. 
We create a dataset with controlled context variations and investigate the effect of context on the MS COCO dataset.

Therefore, we recommend selecting an object detector based on the context rather than a deep network architecture.

Our primary objective is to elucidate how the widespread use of embeddings in NLP is influenced by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. We utilize a mathematical framework to highlight the implicit assumptions regarding language structure inherent in this model. Our analysis reveals that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are formed and how they capture frequentist synonyms. These assumptions enable the creation of generative models and an explicit analysis of the commonly used loss function in NLP. Additionally, we generate synthetic corpora with varying levels of structure and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the word2vec algorithm in learning them. We also empirically evaluate the ability of these models to capture structures in a large corpus of financial news, spanning 12 years and comprising 42 million articles. Our analysis relies on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists, which are widely used in financial text analysis. We show that embeddings can mistakenly treat antonyms as frequentist synonyms, leading to the mixing of terms with opposing polarity. Furthermore, we investigate the non-stationarity of the financial corpus, a phenomenon that has not been extensively documented in the literature. Our analysis involves time-series analysis of cosine similarity between groups of polarized words or company names, revealing that embeddings capture a complex mix of English semantics and word distributions that are difficult to disentangle.

Infective to Recovered (SIR) epidemic model on a social network is conducted. These clusters exhibit distinct and complex dynamics when compared to on-site clusters in non-interacting particle systems. Unlike on-site pairs, nearest-neighbor dimers behave as interacting particles that perform a unique quantum walk in a different lattice structure, resulting in a dynamic characterized by multiple time scales. This connection between the anomalous slow dynamics of these models and flat-band physics can be directly observed in experiments using lanthanide atoms.

A new study proposes an alternative approach, which involves using new observable indicators to indirectly identify ultra-high energy photons through cosmic ray phenomena consisting of extensive air showers or primary cosmic rays observed simultaneously. This study utilizes simulations of ultra-high energy photons interacting with the Sun's magnetic field, incorporating essential modifications to the PRESHOWER program. The expected outcome of these interactions is the creation of cosmic ray ensembles in the form of extremely thin and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the entire cosmic ray energy spectrum. Upon entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components can generate distinctive patterns of spatially correlated extensive air showers, which can also occur when primary ultra-high energy photons are not directed towards the Earth. The particle distributions within these multi-primary ultra-high energy photon footprints are anticipated to have thicknesses of approximately meters and elongations reaching hundreds of millions of kilometers, making them potentially observable with a global, multi-experiment approach, including the re-examination of historical data. The expected event rate exceeds the capabilities of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The methods described in this report enable the simulation of observable quantities related to cosmic ray ensembles induced by ultra-high energy photons, including densities, energy spectra, and geographical orientations of particles at the top of the Earth's atmosphere.

-mass stellar objects may be impacted by rotation due to the influence of centrifugal force and the resulting shape distortion. For stars below a critical mass, centrifugal force can counteract gravitational pull, potentially preventing collapse. However, for those above the critical mass, rapid rotation may lead to the separation of material, as indicated by the Roche lobe model. Using a simplified approach, we examine the effects of rotation on the stability of low-mass stars with sustainable hydrogen burning, focusing on objects smaller than the Sun. Our analysis assumes that all angular momentum is deposited at the equator and utilizes the Roche lobe model to calculate the critical angular momentum necessary for stable hydrogen burning. By combining this with the relationship between angular momentum and spin period, we derive constraints on the spin periods of low-mass stars undergoing sustainable hydrogen burning. These constraints suggest that the maximum spin period for sustainable hydrogen burning in objects around 0.25 to 0.50 solar masses is approximately 10 to 20 minutes, with the exact value depending on the star's mass. This is significantly shorter than the periods found in classical T Tauri stars, which typically range from a few hours to several days. Our research also indicates that purely radial pulsations and bar modes may be used to detect exoplanets orbiting low-mass stars with sustainable hydrogen burning.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications and are often represented graphically as a 2-tier layout, where each group is displayed as a set of nodes on separate horizontal lines, and the relationships between them are depicted by lines connecting corresponding nodes on the two lines. One key goal in creating these visualizations is to minimize the number of intersecting lines, but achieving this is computationally intensive and may still result in cluttered layouts that compromise their clarity. We explore a recent method to eliminate these intersections by relocating nodes, aiming to identify the minimum number of nodes that need to be relocated to produce an uncluttered layout. Our research demonstrates that determining whether a clear layout can be achieved by relocating no more than $k$ nodes is computationally efficient in relation to $k$.

Nonetheless, there are still several challenges to overcome, including the ability to process continuous visual data and the issue of class imbalance in datasets. Current research addresses these issues separately, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this study, we focus on the problem of learning incrementally from datasets with class imbalance. We concentrate on algorithms that maintain a consistent deep model complexity and utilize a limited memory capacity to store examples from previous classes across incremental stages. Given the limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer images than new classes, resulting in an imbalance that combines with the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a bias towards new classes emerges, and we assess a range of score calibration methods to mitigate it. Evaluations were conducted using three datasets, with two imbalance configurations and three memory capacity settings. The results indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial effects and are particularly useful in scenarios with lower memory constraints, which are more relevant in practice. Additionally, we demonstrate that removing the distillation component from the loss function of incremental learning algorithms can lead to improved performance, making vanilla fine-tuning a more effective approach for handling imbalanced incremental learning.

research introduces a new technique called HyperDegrade, which combines existing methods with the use of multi-threading architectures.  In addition to this new technique, the study identifies the underlying causes of performance degradation through cache eviction and uncovers a previously unknown source of slowdown. The resulting slowdown is significantly higher than previous methods, leading to a finer time granularity for Flush+Reload attacks. The effectiveness of HyperDegrade is demonstrated on various Intel microarchitectures, yielding substantial slowdowns that achieve significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods. To evaluate the effectiveness of performance degradation in side-channel amplification, the study proposes and evaluates metrics for assessing information leakage. Furthermore, the study conducts a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies in conjunction with Flush+Reload attacks from an attacker's perspective. It is demonstrated that HyperDegrade excels in an attack on an unexploited OpenSSL vulnerability, requiring three times fewer Flush+Reload traces to succeed. The study also revisits the Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges and demonstrates its application to other protocols using HyperDegrade, which enables an end-to-end attack with real data.

Although the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment is minimal, a bottom-up EFT analysis reveals that the Higgs could still provide a viable solution to the anomaly, given current experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, if its interactions with other SM particles deviate from SM predictions. machine learning technique, where various parties can jointly train a robust model

classified into horizontal and vertical FL. Horizontal FL involves participants

Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily relies on ventricular volume and function according to current clinical guidelines. These biomarkers can be accurately assessed through 3D cardiac magnetic resonance image segmentation. Recent studies have shown that U-Net architectures have achieved impressive results on various datasets. However, in real-world clinical settings, data sets are more diverse and influenced by individual pathologies, scanner properties, and limited training data for rare conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot. This work investigates two aspects: the accuracy gap when training models on one dataset (ACDC) and applying them to another (TOF), and whether similar results can be achieved when applying models to a more heterogeneous dataset. Multiple deep learning models were trained and evaluated using four-fold cross-validation, demonstrating that models can achieve excellent results within a single dataset but struggle with overfitting when applied to other pathologies, resulting in significantly reduced dice scores for both left and right ventricles.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), have been facing a long-standing challenge. FPNs generally improve detection performance but often at the expense of large-scale objects. This paper investigates the impact of FPNs on detection frameworks from an optimization perspective. It identifies the root cause of the suppressed performance of large-scale objects as the creation of improper back-propagation paths after integrating FPNs. This limitation restricts each level of the backbone network to focus on objects within a specific scale range. To address this issue, two strategies are proposed. Firstly, auxiliary objective functions are introduced to enable each backbone level to receive signals from various-scale objects during training. Secondly, a more rational approach to constructing the feature pyramid is proposed to eliminate irrational back-propagation paths. Experimental results on the COCO benchmark validate the analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, achieving significant improvements of over 2% in various detection frameworks.

To address this issue, we introduce a new approach called Dual-Gated Mechanism (DM), which treats the action boundary as a dual variable that can be optimized rather than a fixed point. Typically, the formation of PTMs following edge localized modes (ELM) is attributed to magnetic field ergodisation and the emergence of a seed magnetic island. This study, however, proposes an alternative explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A notable feature of plasma turbulence is the presence of coherent, long-lived structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. These localized, magnetic-field-aligned regions exhibit varying plasma densities and carry parallel currents. By interpreting ELM filaments as massive blobs and the interspace between them as holes, the study demonstrates that a closed current filament can produce magnetic fluctuations similar to those measured by the JET in-vessel magnetic pickup coils when a PTM is present. This suggests that capturing a hole on a q=3 surface after an ELM crash can generate a PTM equivalent signature, while capturing the ELM filament itself on a q=4 surface can produce an outer mode signature.

The annealed large deviation principle for the empirical process of words involves a rate function that is the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words relative to the reference distribution of words. In a previous study, the quenched large deviation principle, which is conditional on a typical letter sequence, was derived for renewal times with an algebraic tail. This resulted in a rate function consisting of two terms, one being the annealed rate function and the other proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. The proportionality constant was the tail exponent of the renewal process. This paper aims to extend both large deviation principles to non-i.i.d. letter sequences by demonstrating that they carry over when the sequence satisfies a mixing condition called summable variation. The rate functions are again specific relative entropies relative to the reference distribution of words or letters, but several approximation arguments are necessary to achieve this extension due to the non-i.i.d. nature of these reference laws.

growing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link.

A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by introducing minimal or no updates to the backbone models during the training process. This paper challenges the necessity of complex models in achieving high performance by comparing them to a simple baseline. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can be a robust tool for achieving competitive or superior continual learning results on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. This baseline is single-headed, exemplar-free, and can be task-free, with the means being updated continually. This variability undermines the reliability of parameter tuning, as the selected parameters are highly susceptible to the partitioning method used. Consequently, optimal parameters are frequently overlooked, and reproducibility is severely compromised. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of J-k-fold cross-validation, which involves conducting J independent k-fold cross-validations to evaluate model performance. Our contributions extend this method from performance estimation to parameter tuning, and we derive the optimal J and k that minimize both bias and variance in the estimated optimal parameters. In comparison with linear and spiral sampling methods, rCASPR was evaluated using in silico, phantom, and in vivo experiments for its point-spread-function and image contrast. This phenomenon reaches its maximum intensity at a specific temperature and magnetic field strength, which likely corresponds to the point where the entropy difference between the central region of the vortex and its surroundings is most pronounced. Notably, the magnitude of this peak is strikingly consistent across a wide range of superconducting materials, suggesting a common underlying mechanism. This peak can be interpreted as the point at which the ratio of viscosity to entropy density within the vortex liquid is minimized. When expressed in terms of the fundamental constants $\hbar$ and $k_B$, this minimum is found to be significantly larger than what is observed in ordinary liquids. Furthermore, the entropy stored within the central region of the vortex is distinct from that associated with a moving magnetic field line, due to the exchange of normal particles that can occur between the vortex and its surroundings. As a result, a slowly moving vortex will tend to lose its associated entropy over a distance comparable to the coherence length of the superconducting material, provided that the ratio of the energy gap to the Fermi energy is sufficiently large.

The interactions between the stars and the surrounding layer cause the orbit to contract. This phase can ultimately lead to the merging of the stars or a subsequent series of interactions. Mergers involving compact objects, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, can produce a range of spectacular astrophysical events, including supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and gravitational waves. Due to the diversity of potential combinations of stars and surrounding layers, common envelope phases cannot be accurately modeled using a single set of parameters. In order to better understand these systems, researchers have been using hydrodynamic simulations to model binary star interactions, including a recent model of a common envelope phase involving a giant star and a neutron star. This model, which considers the effects of angular momentum and heat generated by friction, was used to study the behavior of a particular binary star system. The results of this study, which involved a large, Sun-like giant star and a classic neutron star, indicated that the neutron star's entry into the giant star's layer would not result in the star's disruption. Instead, the model predicted that the neutron star would eventually become trapped at the center of the giant star's remaining layer, provided that the giant star's momentum was sufficient to overcome certain thresholds. This scenario is believed to be a possible explanation for the giant star's behavior in the famous binary system PS

Currently, there are limited methods for assessing Linked Data quality, which often struggle to handle large datasets and become computationally impractical. In this paper, we introduce DistQualityAssessment, a distributed, in-memory quality assessment framework for large RDF datasets, built on Apache Spark. This innovative approach enables scalable quality metric computation and provides a pattern for generating new metrics applicable to big data. Integrated with the SANSA framework, our method has been successfully applied to multiple use cases beyond the SANSA community, demonstrating its superiority in terms of generality, efficiency, and scalability compared to existing approaches.

As alternative non-parametric approaches can be inefficient, this paper introduces a robust method for estimating parameters in models of stochastic processes, leveraging the strengths of the density power divergence measure. time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) lies in maintaining the integrity of specific properties inherent to the continuous solution, such as underlying conservation laws or geometric structures. Researchers have been studying structure-preserving discretisation schemes for a considerable amount of time, including verifying that conventional methods retain these properties and proposing innovative schemes that achieve both high accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the underlying differential equation. However, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, these schemes have a significant drawback - their ability to preserve structure relies on the exact solution of the systems of equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. Although this is feasible for small systems, it becomes impractical for large linear systems resulting from typical discretisation of space-time PDEs. This paper proposes an adjustment to the flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that enforces selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions, and demonstrates its application to both conservation laws and dissipative systems.

To ensure safe braking distances, it is essential to detect obstacles beyond a certain range. However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining accurate annotations for far-field objects, particularly with lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Moreover, current evaluation metrics for 3D detection are not tailored to the specific needs of far-field objects, which can lead to an incomplete analysis of this task. For instance, the conventional wisdom that high-resolution RGB sensors are essential for detecting far-away objects has been disputed by recent results showing that lidar-based methods still perform better on current benchmark leaderboards. To address this gap, we have developed a method to create a well-annotated far-field validation set from the nuScenes dataset and proposed a new evaluation protocol for far-field 3D detection. Our experiments demonstrate the importance of high-resolution RGB sensors in improving 3D detection in the far-field and also introduce a novel fusion method that combines detections from RGB and lidar detectors, achieving state-of-the-art performance in far-field detection.

the potential energy surface (PES) of molecules, which represents their energy levels in relation to their nuclear positions. Nevertheless, calculating this data is complex due to the vast number of ground states and the high computational requirements for excited states. This research introduces a novel approach using a generative quantum machine learning model to prepare quantum simulations for any point on the PES by providing quantum data, such as wave functions and energies, in the form of classical parameters. This is achieved by training a non-expandable unitary coupled model to optimize simulations using a few optimizable parameters, which dramatically reduces the computational time compared to conventional methods. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we applied it to the hydrogen chain, a simple model consisting of two to 10 hydrogen atoms, and a more complex scenario involving the ground and excited states of a methane molecule. Our results show that this quantum machine learning model can efficiently produce high-quality documents, including wave functions and energies, for any nuclear configuration within the PES bounds. Furthermore, this approach significantly enhances the practicality of simulations by enabling the preparation of simulations with a limited number of quantum circuits, consisting of around 50 to 70 parametric quantum gates, in place of the numerous qubit swaps traditionally required.

The liver's lack of distinct features and imaging modality noise make correspondence establishment particularly challenging. To address this issue, we introduce a 3D scene flow benchmark and a novel self-supervised training framework. The benchmark comprises datasets that progressively increase in complexity, from a single moving object to real-world environments. We also propose Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised flow estimation, where two models work in tandem: one estimates motion vectors from point cloud sequences, and the other learns a latent metric to differentiate between translated points and the target point cloud. This concept, initially explored in the 1970s, combines properties of matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and edge colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs and aims to identify those where every perfect matching corresponds to a colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. This is equivalent to determining whether such graphs are even-2-factorable, meaning all their 2-factors consist solely of even cycles. Since bipartite cubic graphs are trivially even-2-factorable, we concentrate on non-bipartite cubic graphs. A cubic graph with the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property is a sufficient but not necessary condition for being even-2-factorable. This work introduces a family of even-2-factorable non-bipartite cubic graphs, known as papillon graphs, and examines the parameters for which these graphs possess the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property or are simply even-2-factorable. Additionally, we prove that papillon graphs with different parameters are never isomorphic.

Unlike traditional static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops effectively handles programs written in languages such as PHP, Python, and JavaScript, and it achieves this with a minimalistic and reliable implementation. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields.

By selectively pumping a nonlinear resonator with a coherent field, we induce a chiral interaction between the resonators, allowing us to create an all-optical diode and a three-port circulator. This chiral coupling enables our device to work with both single-photon pulses and strong light, offering an isolation ratio of over 40 dB and fidelity of more than 98%. Moreover, we've demonstrated the ability to switch nonreciprocal transmission on and off with a relatively weak pump light, effectively creating an optical transistor. Our approach provides a novel path to designing compact, chip-compatible nonreciprocal optical devices for isolating and processing quantum information.

While the quality of generated language is often assessed through semantic and syntactic evaluations, the representation of the input encoder is frequently overlooked. This oversight is problematic since the encoder's representation plays a crucial role in predicting the correct response. In this work, we demonstrate that relying solely on human or automatic metrics to evaluate text generation is insufficient for assessing a dialogue model's understanding of language. To address this limitation, we propose a set of probe tasks to evaluate the encoder representation of various language encoders used in dialogue models. Our experiments reveal that some probe tasks are more challenging for even advanced model architectures to master. Interestingly, our findings suggest that RNN-based architectures outperform transformer models on certain probe tasks, indicating that RNNs might retain task-specific information more effectively.

However, extracting robust and efficient 3D LiDAR descriptors that remain invariant to changing conditions and orientation remains a challenge. To address this issue, a novel deep learning network called AttDLNet is proposed, which leverages a range-based proxy representation and an attention mechanism to selectively focus on long-range context and inter-feature relationships. As video streaming demands surge, Streaming Service Providers are increasingly relying on cloud services to ensure Quality of Service. Cloud providers offer various Virtual Machines with differing prices, prompting the use of resource provisioning to optimize cost efficiency. To achieve this, provisioning involves renting the most appropriate VM with the precise characteristics for a specific workload, such as video transcoding, and either sacrificing some quality for a lower cost or producing higher quality output for a higher cost. This paper introduces a method for predicting the performance of a video transcoding application on different cloud VMs using machine learning. By accurately predicting the transcoding time on each VM, the most cost-effective VM can be identified, allowing for the optimal VM to be provisioned for various video streams with different requirements. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, showing that it is possible to achieve up to 28% cost savings while maintaining the desired quality of service. This method can be applied to other cloud applications with modification.

As a result, they struggle to generate high-quality paragraph-level speech that demands expressiveness and naturalness. To address this, a context-aware speech synthesis system called MaskedSpeech is proposed, which incorporates both contextual semantic and acoustic features. MaskedSpeech draws inspiration from speech editing techniques, masking current sentence acoustic features and combining them with contextual speech, then using the result as additional input. The phoneme encoder learns contextual text information from neighboring sentences, and cross-utterance speech synthesis is achieved by conditioning the generator on contextual speech and the masked acoustic features of the current sentence. MaskedSpeech is trained to minimize a perceived speech edit distance, comprising text-to-speech synthesis errors and speech-to-text transcription errors. Experimental results show that MaskedSpeech significantly outperforms the baseline system in terms of naturalness and expressiveness.

inaccuracies in contextualized embedding-based methods for identifying semantic shifts in words over time. We introduce a new ensemble approach that surpasses existing contextualized methods, which we use to investigate the predicted semantic changes in English words across a 50-year period. Our analysis reveals that contextualized methods often mistakenly flag words with significant change scores, even when they are not experiencing genuine semantic evolution. We delve into specific cases and propose a classification system for these challenging instances. Our findings indicate that pre-trained contextualized language models are prone to conflating changes in word meanings and contextual fluctuations, inherent to their distributional nature, as well as merging semantic and syntactic aspects of words. We suggest potential future solutions to address these limitations.

This can be achieved by utilizing the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship connecting radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. In this study, we utilized long-term, high-speed imaging techniques to visualize zebrafish retinas in real-time during early development, aiming to uncover the underlying mechanisms governing nuclear behavior during this process. Our high-resolution images enabled us to accurately track the movement and division of numerous tightly packed nuclei, which were then used to develop and test a theoretical model of retinal IKNM as a diffusive process driven by a concentration gradient of nuclei at the upper layer. Our analysis revealed the impact of nuclear density at the upper layer on the migration dynamics of nuclei, provided reliable estimates for the rate constants of nuclear migration and division, confirmed the previously proposed idea that nuclei at the upper layer have a higher chance of dividing in place, and offered insights into the role of these factors in determining the overall nuclear density distribution within the retina.

Practical code patterns in these applications are typically non-negative, structured, and often deviate from the incoherence properties of patterns like Gaussian codes, which can negatively impact reconstruction performance. This paper contributes to the design of code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing by minimizing the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi \Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ is the signal representation matrix. understanding exoplanet properties. Although Kepler and TESS missions have shown that planets are widespread, these missions rely on ground-based observations for detailed information. The TESS-Keck Survey aims to investigate the relationships between stellar properties and exoplanet compositions, as well as system architectures, by combining TESS data and Keck IR resources. The survey targets small planets around nearby bright stars that can be studied using a range of techniques. We present target selection criteria and describe the properties of these planets, which include systems with multiple planets, systems with planets near or inside the habitable zone, small planets orbiting low-mass stars, and planets orbiting stars with known chemical abundances. The survey will investigate themes such as planetary system configurations, relationships between stellar and planetary properties, the effectiveness of detection methods, and the reliability of measured planetary densities. The survey will also contribute to the development of targets for future missions like TESS 2 and JWST. The TESS-Keck Survey provides a framework for combining large astronomical datasets and investigating the most promising exoplanet systems.

Researchers have developed empirical relationships using observable data to estimate stellar properties, often in the form of non-linear functions. However, Bayesian modeling requires the opposite approach. This article introduces a novel Bayesian framework that integrates multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, radius, and surface temperature of field age M-dwarfs. The framework includes a new mass-radius relationship with a low 3.1% margin of error. The study also introduces the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), which is comprised of nearby low-mass stars with available ultraviolet spectroscopic data. The researchers applied their methodology to these targets, which are of interest due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across various wavelengths. By analyzing the field MUSS stars, the authors defined the low-mass main sequence in the solar neighborhood using Gaussian Process regression. This enabled them to identify a characteristic feature in the GP derivative at a mass of approximately 0.337 M$_{\odot}$, which marks the transition from fully to partly convective interiors within the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample.

Two key theories attempt to explain this animacy continuum: the visual categorization theory proposes that it is driven by the presence of animal-specific characteristics, while the agency theory suggests that it is rooted in how animals are perceived as agents. In this study, we investigated these hypotheses by creating a stimulus set that isolated visual categorizability and agency, and then used fMRI to analyze how they contributed to the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex. Our results indicate that both visual categorizability and agency play distinct roles in shaping the animacy continuum, and that together they fully account for its complexity. Furthermore, our data show that visual categorizability and agency have different spatial representations within the ventral temporal cortex, with visual categorizability localized more posteriorly than agency. These findings demonstrate that multiple factors, including agency, contribute to the organization of the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex.

Our customized approach has enabled us to obtain radii for 6097 clusters, representing the largest sample available to date. The study reveals that a significant number of galaxies exhibit a common cluster radius distribution, peaking at approximately 3 parsecs. It consists of two key instruments: the VIS and the NISP, the latter of which comprises detectors that will be affected by correlated readout noise during in-flight measurements. We have developed an analytical expression to quantify the noise covariance matrix in the presence of correlated noise, specifically in the MACC readout mode. We have also characterized the properties of correlated readout noise in the NISP engineering-grade detectors using long dark integrations, finding that it follows a (1/f)^α noise model with typical parameters. Through realistic simulations, we have estimated the bias in flux measurements resulting from correlated readout noise and found that using our analytical expression for the covariance matrix reduces this bias by up to four times compared to the white noise approximation. Ultimately, we conclude that even with the white noise approximation, the bias on NISP flux measurements will be negligible.

Consequently, identifying and controlling the spread of online rumors has become an urgent priority. To address this, we investigated the mechanisms behind rumor dissemination and developed a method to measure the impact of a rumor based on its propagation speed. The frequency of searches related to the rumor served as a key indicator. By analyzing the peak and attenuation rates, which follow an exponential distribution, we identified crucial features and applied them to a predictive model. Our results, obtained through a 5-fold cross-validation experiment, revealed that decision trees are effective for predicting peak rates, while linear regression models perform best for predicting attenuation rates. Our analysis also highlighted the significance of precursor features in determining the peak rate, whereas location and entity information are more relevant for predicting the attenuation rate. Notably, features that facilitate the initial spread of a rumor often hinder its continued dissemination. Additionally, anxiety was found to be a critical factor contributing to the spread of rumors. Finally, we discuss the potential of utilizing the BERT model to minimize forecast errors and improve the accuracy of rumor prediction.

omechanical behavior in unfilled polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The crystallization process significantly affects a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, necessitating consideration in manufacturing and application design. To comprehensively capture its effects, the proposed model employs a novel approach that involves decomposing the deformation gradient into three components and utilizes the Coleman-Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle for material modeling. The chosen framework yields equations capable of simulating crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic tensile testing. The resulting boundary value problem, which includes linear momentum and energy balance, serves as the basis for numerical implementation in a finite element method (FEM) code. The paper concludes with numerical examples illustrating microstructure evolution and temperature distribution in various material samples.

This research examines how these discoveries impact the formation of black-hole-neutron-star binaries, including the potential candidate event GW190426_152155, as well as the influence of natal kicks and neutron-star radii on the creation of such systems and their associated electromagnetic counterparts. Models based on detailed simulations predict a significantly higher rate of merger detections for black-hole-neutron-star systems, with rates up to five to ten times higher than those predicted by traditional methods. This increased detection rate is primarily due to the formation of low-mass black holes through direct collapse, resulting in negligible natal kicks. The likelihood of observed systems producing an electromagnetic counterpart varies between two to twenty-five percent, depending on uncertainties in the neutron-star equation of state. Furthermore, simulations suggest that in most merging systems with electromagnetic counterparts, the neutron star is the first-born compact object, provided its radius is less than 12 kilometers. Core-collapse models that predict the formation of low-mass black holes with negligible natal kicks increase the distance at which GW190426_152155's electromagnetic counterpart can be observed, from 2.6 to 4.5 gigaparsecs, significantly impacting the expected sky localization of fast radio bursts and the associated cosmic ray emission.

This was achieved by analyzing the noise kernels associated with the stress-energy tensor of quantum fields. In this study, we revisit this topic by employing a quantum thermodynamics approach, which involves calculating key thermodynamic parameters: heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. This paper posits that rain generation and removal are interconnected processes that should be addressed simultaneously. To achieve this, we propose a unified image translation framework that learns to generate and remove rain simultaneously. The framework consists of a bidirectional translation network, where each direction involves two cycles of joint rain generation and removal for both real and synthetic rain images. To enforce the separation of background and rain layers, we utilize both cycle-consistency and adversarial losses. Conversely, a counterpart composition with the entanglement strategy is applied for rain generation. Our proposed method has been extensively tested on both synthetic and real-world rain datasets, demonstrating its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Nevertheless, certain components of HHL are incompatible with Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid formulation of HHL that enables the end-to-end execution of small-scale portfolio-optimization problems on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variant with new quantum-hardware capabilities, including mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). Notably, NISQ-HHL incorporates a QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation executed on real hardware, the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, marking a significant innovation. Furthermore, NISQ-HHL features a novel approach for determining the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian simulation. Although this research focuses on portfolio optimization, the proposed techniques to improve HHL's scalability are universally applicable to any problem that can be solved via HHL in the NISQ era.

Specifically, we have found that the assumption is valid for nanowires with a switching probability greater than 10^-2, but is no longer valid for the two nanowires with a high standard deviation that were previously studied. We have also determined that the critical voltages at which the nanowires switch on and off are bimodal, with the secondary mode occurring at a critical voltage that is significantly higher than the primary mode. unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following points are addressed: 

- Enhancements: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security under minimal assumptions, available for both public-key and private-key settings.
- Limitations: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a cloning attack with a probability of success of $0.85^n$. A broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is used to generalize the construction, and a $0.75^n$ cloning attack is demonstrated against their scheme.
- Implications: Unclonable encryption satisfying a stronger property, unclonable-indistinguishability, implies copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Although current encryption schemes do not satisfy this property, this connection provides a new path to construct copy-protection.

The analysis involves a model comprising an encoder, decoder, and adversary, with the latter having access to the message, a non-causal noisy representation of the transmission, and unlimited transmission capabilities. The decoder receives a noisy sum of the encoder and adversary's outputs. A method to adapt existing channel codes for authentication is proposed, and it's shown that this modification incurs an infinitesimally small rate cost while enabling authentication as long as the adversary's observation isn't noiseless. Building on these findings, the study calculates the channel-authenticated capacity and shows it's equivalent to the non-adversarial channel capacity. This modular approach, designed for the specified channel model, is applicable to a broad range of scenarios.

The presence of lattice relaxation in the sample causes the flat band to blend with remote valence bands, leading to significant differences in the contribution of interband transitions to the plasmon dispersion and energy. Under conditions where only intraband transitions within the doped flat band are considered, low-damped and quasi-flat plasmons arise. Conversely, a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion is observed when interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands are also taken into account. The plasmon energies can be adjusted through twist angles and doping levels. However, in rigid samples without lattice relaxation, both lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons can coexist. For highly doped rigid samples, enhanced interband transitions can suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Our study highlights the importance of two key factors, the isolated flat band and a suitable hole-doping level, for observing the low-damped and quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides. The findings of this research may provide valuable insights for studying plasmon-mediated superconductivity in these materials in the future.

This study centers on agreement prediction in Basque, serving as a case study for a task requiring an implicit comprehension of sentence structure and the acquisition of a complex yet systematic morphological system. Our analysis of experimental outcomes from two syntactic prediction tasks - verb number prediction and suffix recovery - reveals that sequential models perform less effectively on Basque agreement prediction than anticipated based on prior agreement prediction research in English. Preliminary findings from diagnostic classifiers suggest that the network relies on local heuristics as a substitute for the hierarchical structure of the sentence. Consequently, we propose the Basque agreement prediction task as a demanding benchmark for models striving to identify regularities in human language.

To reduce radiation exposure, PET scans can be taken with lower doses or shorter acquisition times, but this can compromise image quality.  Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the creation of high-quality PET images from low-quality scans, often in conjunction with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data.  However, current deep learning methods are typically designed to perform well on test data with characteristics similar to the training data, but they often fail when applied to new, out-of-distribution data.  We introduce a novel deep learning framework that incorporates the physics underlying PET imaging and estimates the uncertainty in its predictions, allowing it to produce high-quality PET images from low-dose scans and MRI data.  Our approach, suDNN, is more robust to out-of-distribution data and outperforms existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, as demonstrated by results from in vivo PET-MRI scans and various forms of out-of-distribution data.

However, determining the spatial distance between these fingerprints is often influenced by signal distance metrics, which in turn are affected by the chosen fingerprint collection method. This paper investigates the effect of motion on WiFi fingerprints and introduces the concept of a signal space that underlies all geospatial analysis. searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through the SETI initiative, with a key focus on identifying Dyson Spheres - massive energy-gathering structures surrounding stars that support advanced civilizations. This study examines the feasibility of constructing a Dyson Sphere around a black hole, considering six potential energy sources, including the cosmic microwave background and relativistic jets. It is estimated that a Dyson Sphere would require at least $4\times10^{26}\,{\rm W}$ to support a Type II civilization. Our analysis indicates that an accretion disk would be the most effective energy source, with a luminosity of $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, and that collecting additional energy types could increase the total energy by approximately fivefold. Furthermore, our results suggest that a Dyson Sphere surrounding a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way would be detectable via waste heat in various wavelengths, including gamma-rays, X-rays, and optical light, making it potentially identifiable using current telescopes such as Fermi-GAMET and LIGO's binary black hole mergers.

A method to achieve this involves using active measurement tools that inject artificial traffic and assess network performance through probes. However, these tools consume a lot of resources and can only cover a small portion of what could be measured, which can lead to missing SLA breaches. The definition of this limited scope is currently handled by human administrators, who lack the scalability and adaptability needed for dynamic networks. This article explores the potential benefits of using peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the detection of SLA breaches. Firstly, we outline the principles of steering active measurement tools using P2P technology, which is characterized by a high degree of decentralized decision-making across a network through a self-organizing overlay. Secondly, we present measurement session activation strategies based on these principles, which do not require human intervention, are adaptable to network condition changes, and independent of the underlying active measurement technology.

, cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on comprehensive models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. However, these models contribute significantly to the systematic uncertainty in these experiments due to limitations in detecting final state neutrons in previous detectors. The upcoming generation of long-baseline neutrino experiments features near detectors consisting of three-dimensional scintillator trackers, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity, enabling them to measure neutron kinetic energy in real-time for each interaction. This capability will significantly enhance neutrino interaction models and energy reconstruction methods. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone testing at the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory in 2019 and 2020, exposing them to neutron energies ranging from 0 to 800 MeV. To validate their neutron detection capabilities, researchers have measured the total neutron-scintillator cross section and compared it to external data, finding a total cross section of 0.36 ± 0.05 barn between 98 and 688 MeV.

In this study, we investigated how the presence of surface water impacts these particles. Typically, laboratory conditions involve multiple water layers on the grains, but in the low-pressure environment of protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only have a single water layer. As dust moves inward, even this layer eventually evaporates in higher temperature zones. To account for this, we re-examined the tensile strength of the same chondritic material we previously studied under normal laboratory conditions, but this time using two new preparation methods: drying the dust in air (dry samples) and heating it in a vacuum (super-dry samples). For temperatures up to 1000 K, our data for dry samples showed that their sticking forces increased by approximately ten times compared to wet samples. Up to 900 K, super-dry samples behaved similarly to dry samples. However, their sticking forces then increased exponentially to another factor of approximately 100 at about 1200 K. The increase in sticking from wet to dry samples follows a trend observed in amorphous silicates and extends to multimineral mixtures. The findings for super-dry dust suggest that aggregate growth is enhanced in a small, high-temperature region around 1200 K, which could be a favorable environment for planetesimal formation.

Unlike unconstrained methods that disregard environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows for adapting human skills to unstructured environments, thus expanding its applicability. Despite the exploration of various constraints, such as joint limits and obstacle avoidance, nonlinear hard constraints remain inadequately addressed. To address these limitations, we introduce extended kernelized movement primitives (EKMP), a framework that tackles the core issues in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn the probabilistic characteristics of multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to desired positions and velocities, avoid obstacles, and satisfy both linear and nonlinear constraints. Additionally, we discuss the connections between EKMP and state-of-the-art motion planning techniques, providing evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm.

In this work, we calculate the one-loop six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, focusing on the central next-to-multi-Regge kinematic limit. We demonstrate that its dispersive part can be expressed in terms of the two-gluon central emission vertex and use this to derive the one-loop two-gluon central emission vertex for all helicity configurations within this theory, which contributes to the two-gluon central emission vertex in QCD. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we show that Rashba coupling and Zeeman field induce a shift in the weight of low-energy quasiparticles and significantly influence the spatial pair correlation function. Finally, we discuss how Rashba coupling and Zeeman field impact topologically non-Abelian states and a finite net magnetization gap, which could be useful for implementing a topological quantum computation.

However, the parabolic model falls short in describing polymers grafted to concave or curved surfaces such as spherical particles or interfaces of block copolymers. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a boundary layer devoid of free chain ends, requiring modifications to the theoretical analysis. Although the "end exclusion zone" has been successfully integrated into models of brushes on the outer surfaces of cylinders and spheres, the behavior of brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature remains unexplored. This study develops a formulation of the strong-stretching theory for molten brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature and identifies four distinct regimes where brushes are predicted to exhibit end exclusion zones, including regimes with positive mean curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we report the predicted scaling of the end exclusion zone size, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching with mean and Gaussian surface curvatures. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how brush geometry influences end exclusion zones and exact strong-stretching free energies, which can be applied to model the full range of brush geometries encountered in block copolymer assembly.

To achieve this, we consider a basic model where multiple agents are instructed to act in a predetermined order, known as the action sequence. Each agent aims to maximize her value based on the actions taken by the preceding agents in the sequence. Our primary objective is to identify action sequences that yield near-optimal overall value for the agents, often referred to as social welfare. We assume that we have query access to the value that each agent receives when she acts after a specific set of agents. We establish strict limits on the social welfare that can be achieved using a polynomial number of queries, and these bounds hold for a broad category of combinatorial optimization problems, encompassing bipartite matching, graph pairing, and single-source shortest paths. However, we found that the social welfare achieved by using a optimal action sequence is significantly better than the known bounds for specific cases of combinatorial optimization. We also discuss implications of our findings for mechanisms with limited truth-telling incentives and provide a lower bound for social welfare against a specific class of action sequences.

By analyzing the deformation of the Central and West African rift zone, we can infer the pre-breakup history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins. Our research indicates that the development of marginal structures like the Pre-salt sag basin and the S\~ao Paulo High is linked to changes in the direction and speed of continental extension. Initially, the rift zone experienced low-velocity E-W extension between South America and Africa until around 126 million years ago, when rift activity in the equatorial Atlantic domain increased significantly. During this initial 17 million-year period, the Pre-salt basin width on the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins was formed. A subsequent stage, lasting from 126.57 million years to the Base Aptian period, was characterized by strain localization, rapid lithospheric weakening, and a shift in extension direction to NE-SW. The final breakup between South America and Africa occurred around 113 million years ago in the Santos-Benguela margin segment and around 103 million years ago in the Equatorial Atlantic domain. We propose that this complex rift history plays a primary role in shaping the conjugate passive margin systems and can explain the major tectonic features along the South Atlantic and possibly other passive margins.
